questions.prompt: A colleague mutters «Мы проебали весь бюджет» (my pra-YE-ba-lee VYES' byu-DZHET). What has happened, and how does the prefix tell you?
questions.answer: The budget has been lost or wasted: про- marks passage through, and проебать (pra-ye-BAT') is the perfective verb for losing or squandering something.
questions.distractor: The budget has been exceeded, because про- marks going beyond a limit.
questions.correction: The error is to read про- as 'beyond'. The prefix marks passage through, as in пройти (pray-TEE), 'to go through', and with this root it produces the sense of something being lost in the process. The verb is perfective past plural, the budget is the accusative object, and the sentence reports a completed loss. Exceeding a budget would be a different verb entirely, перерасходовать (pee-ree-ras-KHO-da-vat'), which belongs to neutral register. Lesson 131's four steps, root, prefix, suffix, ending, give the right answer here without a dictionary, because про- plus the transitive frame plus the perfective past points to a completed loss rather than to a limit.

questions.prompt: A friend says «До хуя работы» (da khoo-YA ra-BO-ty). What does the phrase mean, and which case is doing the work?
questions.answer: 'There is a hell of a lot of work': до plus the genitive работы (ra-BO-ty) marks extent, so the phrase measures quantity.
questions.distractor: 'There is hardly any work': до plus the genitive marks a limit that has almost been reached.
questions.correction: The error is to treat до as a limit rather than as an extent. With quantity expressions, до plus the genitive measures how far the quantity goes, as in до края (da KRA-ya), 'to the brim', and in this idiom the measure is deliberately huge. The same pattern appears in до фига (da fee-GA), 'a lot', which lesson 138 treats as the publishable substitute. The genitive is not the genitive of negation and nothing is being denied; the sentence is an emphatic affirmative. If the phrase had been ни хуя работы (nee khoo-YA ra-BO-ty), the ни would make it a categorical denial and the meaning would reverse.

questions.prompt: A message reads «Пиздато отдохнули» (peez-DA-ta at-dakh-NOO-lee). Is this praise or complaint, and what tells you?
questions.answer: Praise: пиздато (peez-DA-ta) is the positive slang adverb 'great', and it modifies the past plural verb отдохнули (at-dakh-NOO-lee), 'had a rest'.
questions.distractor: Complaint: the root is obscene, so the adverb must be negative.
questions.correction: The error is to infer polarity from the root. The пизда family split into two evaluative branches: пиздец (peez-DYETS) is the negative terminal state, and пиздатый (peez-DA-ty) with its adverb пиздато is positive slang meaning 'excellent' and 'great'. The Russian Wiktionary entry for пиздато lists отлично (at-LEECH-na), 'excellently', among its synonyms and хуёво (khoo-YO-va), 'badly', among its antonyms, which settles the polarity. The mistake is expensive because it reverses a compliment. The register remains obscene, so the praise is warm and unpublishable at the same time, which is precisely the combination lesson 133 describes.

questions.prompt: In a meeting a colleague says «Он выебал меня за отчёт» (on VY-ye-bal mee-NYA za at-CHYOT). Which sense is selected, and by what?
questions.answer: The telling-off sense, 'he tore me off a strip about the report', selected by за plus the accusative of reason.
questions.distractor: The literal sexual sense, because выебать (VY-ye-bat') means to have sex with someone.
questions.correction: The error is to keep only one gloss for a verb with two senses. The Russian Wiktionary entry for выебать gives both the literal sense and the sense of swearing at or punishing someone severely, and the deciding evidence is the complement: за plus the accusative отчёт names a reason for a reprimand, which the literal sense cannot take. Remove the reason phrase and the literal reading becomes the default, so «Он выебал её» (on VY-ye-bal ye-YO) is a statement about sex. Lesson 134's point is that these verbs are disambiguated by their complements, not by their form, so the same string of sounds is two different verbs in two different frames.

questions.prompt: A learner writes «Блять, я забыл ключи» (BLYAT', ya za-BYL KLYOO-chee) in an email to a landlord. Which parts of that are wrong, and what is the analysis?
questions.answer: The register is wrong for the recipient, and the spelling блять is the variant dictionaries list as a misspelling of блядь; the word is an expletive with no target, aimed at nobody, in a message that records.
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong: блядь and блять are two different words, and the interjection is acceptable in any written message.
questions.correction: Two errors sit in one sentence. The spelling is the smaller one: English Wiktionary labels блять a misspelling of блядь, and the dictionary form keeps the soft sign in both functions. The larger error is the register, since an email to a landlord is written, institutional and permanent, and the expletive is obscene by the media definition even when it targets nobody. The analysis should also note what the word is doing: comma-separated and removable, it reports the speaker's state rather than insulting the landlord, so the problem is not aggression but audience. Lesson 135 separates the two functions and lesson 137 explains why a written channel converts a harmless expletive into a record.

units.title: Intensity, target and social risk: what a mat word does, who hears it, and what to say when it is aimed at you

lessons.title: One root, two jobs: mat as an intensifier and mat as an insult, and the affixes that shift the force
lessons.explanation:
Every lesson so far has described forms. This one describes the difference between two uses of the same forms, because that difference decides whether a sentence is rude in the way that a spilled coffee is rude or rude in the way that a slap is rude. The first use is the expletive or intensifier: the word reports the speaker's state, marks emphasis, or evaluates a situation, and it has no target. The second is invective: the word is aimed at a person and lowers their standing in front of whoever is present. The two uses draw on the same lexicon, often on the same word, and they are distinguished by syntax rather than by vocabulary.

Syntactically, an expletive sits outside the clause or modifies a predicate. It can be removed without damage, it agrees with nothing, and it takes no arguments. Invective does grammatical work inside the clause. It can be the predicate of a second person pronoun, as in ты хуй (ty KHUY), 'you are a prick'; it can be an apposition to a name, as in «а он, хуй, опять не пришёл» (a on, KHUY, a-PYAT' ne pree-SHYOL), 'and he, the prick, did not turn up again'; it can be an imperative with a directional phrase, as in иди на хуй (ee-DEE na KHUY), 'fuck off'; or it can be a noun of agent, as in хуйло (khooy-LO), 'a contemptible person, an arsehole'. Each of those four frames makes a person the subject of the evaluation, and that is what targeting means.

V. I. Zhelvis's taxonomy of invective functions, summarised in the Russian Wikipedia article on обсценная лексика (ap-STSEN-na-ya LEK-see-ka), 'obscene vocabulary', lists twenty-seven functions, and the list is useful here because it separates the ones that involve a target from the ones that do not. Among them are the cathartic function, which discharges the speaker's tension; the function of lowering the addressee's social status; the function of establishing contact between equals; friendly teasing or encouragement; the use of invective as an interjection; and invective as verbal aggression. The article itself carries a warning that the section may contain original research and that the division is sometimes too fine, so cite the taxonomy as a map rather than as a measurement.

The prefix is the main device for shifting force within one root. за- adds saturation, so заебать (za-ye-BAT') describes an effect on a person's state: the person is worn out, not attacked. на- adds accumulation and deception, so наебать (na-ye-BAT') is an act against a person's interests: they are cheated. до- adds arrival, so доебаться (da-ye-BAT-sa) is an act against a person's peace: they are pestered. вы- adds completion, and выебать (VY-ye-bat') in its second sense is an act against a person's standing: they are torn off a strip in front of others. раз- adds dispersal, so разъебать (raz-ye-BAT') damages a thing rather than a person. про- adds passage, so проебать (pra-ye-BAT') is a loss that usually damages the speaker. Read down that list and the progression is visible: effect on a state, effect on interests, effect on peace, effect on standing, damage to an object. The obscenity is constant; the force moves.

Suffixes do the same work in the nominal system. -ня builds a mass noun, which is why хуйня (khooy-NYA) evaluates stuff rather than a person. -ло builds a contemptuous person noun, which is why хуйло names somebody and хуйня cannot. -ец builds a terminal-state noun, which is why пиздец (peez-DYETS) comments on a situation. -ёж builds a process noun, which is why пиздёж (peez-DYOSH) names the activity of lying rather than a liar. Diminutives and augmentatives are recorded for the пизда root, with пиздёнка (peez-DYON-ka) as the diminutive and пиздища (peez-DEE-shcha) as the augmentative. What those forms change is stance rather than politeness: a diminutive can sound affectionate, ironic or dismissive depending on tone, and it does not lift the taboo for a second. An adult learner who expects a diminutive to make a mat word safe has misunderstood what diminutives do.

The practical consequence is that intensity ratings are the wrong tool. A word can be maximally obscene and socially mild, as блядь is when it is an expletive between colleagues, and a word can be mildly obscene and socially lethal, as a well-aimed хуйло is in a meeting. Obscenity is a property of the lexicon; force is a property of the speech act; and the speech act is determined by the target, the relationship and the audience. That is why this course classifies by target rather than by a numerical scale, and why lesson 140's capstone asks for three labels, target, force and register, instead of a score.
lessons.example:
Five sentences, one root, five targets. «Хуйня этот отчёт.» (khooy-NYA EH-tat at-CHYOT) 'This report is junk.' The noun is the predicate of the report, and the report is a thing. «Меня заебали эти правки.» (mee-NYA za-ye-BA-lee EH-tee PRAF-kee) 'I am worn out by these edits.' The person worn out is in the accusative, the edits are the subject, and the effect is on a state. «Он наебал нас на поставке.» (on na-ye-BAL nas na pa-STAFF-kye) 'He cheated us on the delivery.' The act is against interests, and the verb is transitive with the victims in the accusative. «Ну ты и хуй.» (noo ty ee KHUY) 'You really are a prick.' The noun is the predicate of ты, and the person is the target. «Ну и хуй с ним.» (noo ee KHUY s NEEM) 'To hell with him.' The fixed phrase dismisses a third party without addressing them, and с plus the instrumental marks the person being written off.

Two more forms show the difference between refusal and insult. «Хуй тебе, а не отпуск.» (KHUY tee-BYE, a ne OT-poosk) 'Fat chance of a holiday.' The dative тебе marks the person refused, and the phrase answers a request rather than judging a character; it is hostile in tone and not an insult in form. «Иди на хуй.» (ee-DEE na KHUY) 'Fuck off.' Here the imperative plus the directional phrase is a dismissal addressed directly to the hearer, and it is the most aggressive of the six because it combines an order with contempt. A learner who classifies all six as 'very rude' has learned nothing usable; a learner who can say that the first evaluates a thing, the second describes a state, the third names an act, the fourth insults, the fifth dismisses and the sixth orders has the whole system.
lessons.question: Two colleagues say «Ну ты и хуй» (noo ty ee KHUY) and «Ну и хуй с ним» (noo ee KHUY s NEEM). Which one targets a person, and how does the grammar show it?
lessons.answer: The first targets the hearer: the noun is the predicate of ты. The second dismisses a third party with the fixed phrase хуй с ним, where с plus the instrumental marks someone being written off rather than addressed.
lessons.distractor: Both target a person, because both contain the same obscene noun and the same dismissive particle ну.
lessons.correction: The error is to read force off the vocabulary instead of the syntax. In «Ну ты и хуй» (noo ty ee KHUY), 'you really are a prick' the pronoun ты is the subject and the noun is its predicate, so the sentence assigns a property to the hearer; there is no other reading. In «Ну и хуй с ним» (noo ee KHUY s NEEM), 'to hell with him' the phrase is fixed, the pronoun is ним in the instrumental governed by с, and the person is being discussed rather than addressed. The particle ну appears in both and carries exasperation in both, which is exactly why the learner's shortcut fails: identical particles, identical noun, different speech acts. The diagnostic is whether the sentence has a second person subject or address. If it does, the utterance is invective, and the safe response belongs to lesson 139.

depth.definitions: Five terms organise the lesson. A target is the person an utterance is aimed at, as distinct from the person who hears it. Invective is language that attacks or lowers a target, and its grammar usually involves a predicate of the second person, an apposition, an imperative or an agent noun. An expletive is a word or phrase that expresses the speaker's state without describing anything, and it typically stands outside the clause. Force is the social weight of a speech act, which depends on target and relationship rather than on the obscenity of the words. A diminutive is a suffix that presents something as small or endearing, and an augmentative presents it as large; with mat roots both change stance and neither changes register. Prerequisites are lesson 131 on the root system, lesson 109 on evaluative suffixes, and lesson 25, where a direct dismissal was introduced.
depth.mechanism:
Argument structure is the mechanism that turns a word into an act. A transitive verb with a person in the accusative describes an effect on that person, as заебать and наебать do. A reflexive verb with no object describes a state of the subject, as заебаться does. A noun in the predicate slot of a second person pronoun assigns a property, as ты хуй does. A noun in apposition, set off by commas, comments on a referent without asserting anything, as «а он, хуй, ...» (a on, KHUY, ...), 'and he, the prick, ...' does. An imperative with a directional phrase orders movement, as иди на хуй does, and the direction is what makes it a dismissal rather than a request.

Affixes shift the force along a scale that runs from state to standing. за- and на- produce effects that a person suffers; до- produces an intrusion on a person's peace; вы- in its second sense produces public humiliation; раз- and про- produce damage to objects and to the speaker's own interests. Nominal suffixes decide what kind of thing is being evaluated: a mass, a person, a process, a terminal state. None of these shifts changes the obscenity, which is why the same root can be tolerable in one frame and unforgivable in another.

The third mechanism is audience. The same speech act has different force depending on who is present to hear it, because invective works by lowering status in front of others. An insult delivered in private is a different act from the same words delivered in a meeting, and the difference is not in the sentence. Lesson 137 turns that observation into a procedure.
depth.secondExample:
Take the progression through prefixes in a single invented paragraph about a project. «Мы проебали сроки.» (my pra-YE-ba-lee SRO-kee) 'We lost the deadlines.' The damage is to the speakers' own interests, and the verb is transitive with a thing as its object. «Заказчик нас заебал вопросами.» (za-KASH-cheek nas za-ye-BAL vap-RO-sa-mee) 'The client wore us out with questions.' The effect is on a state, and the instrument is in the instrumental case. «Он доебался до каждой строчки.» (on da-ye-BAL-sya da KAZH-day STROCH-kee) 'He latched on to every single line.' The intrusion is on peace, and the preposition до plus genitive marks the target of the pestering. «Потом выебал нас при всех.» (pa-TOM VY-ye-bal nas pree VSYEKH) 'Then he tore us off a strip in front of everyone.' The humiliation is public, and при всех, 'in front of everyone', is the phrase that makes the force explicit.

Four sentences, four prefixes, one escalating curve: loss, exhaustion, intrusion, public humiliation. Nothing in the root changed, and nothing in the obscenity changed either. What changed is where the act landed and who saw it. That is the analytical content of the lesson, and it is also the reason a learner cannot decide how strong a word is by looking it up.
depth.mistake:
The first error is to treat obscenity as intensity. Learners ask whether a word is 'very strong' and expect a number, but the number depends on the frame: the same word is mild as an expletive and severe as a predicate of the hearer. The diagnostic is to ask who the sentence is about. If the answer is the speaker, the word is an expletive; if it is the hearer, the word is invective, whatever its dictionary label.

The second error is to expect morphology to soften register. Adding a diminutive to a mat root, or choosing the milder member of a family, changes the stance and not the taboo; a diminutive obscenity is still an obscenity, and in some tones it is more patronising than the plain form. The third error is to underestimate apposition. A word set off by commas looks like an aside and reads like a comment, which is why «а он, хуй, ...» (a on, KHUY, ...), 'and he, the prick, ...' can be more wounding than a direct insult: it treats the target as a thing to be characterised rather than an opponent to be addressed.
depth.application:
Use the three-label classification whenever you meet mat in the wild. Name the target, the force and the register, in that order. A comment under a news item reading «ну и хуйня» (noo ee khooy-NYA), 'well, what junk' has no target, evaluates a thing and belongs to the register of anonymous public speech. A message reading «ты хуйло» (ty khooy-LO), 'you are a contemptible arsehole' has a second person target, insults standing and belongs to a private quarrel that has become public if anyone else can see the thread. The labels take ten seconds and they prevent the two common misreadings, which are seeing an insult in every obscenity and seeing a harmless expletive in every familiar word.

For production, the classification is also a filter. If the target is a person and the audience includes anyone who has not consented to the register, the form is unavailable, regardless of how mild it feels. That rule is simpler than a list of permitted words and it scales to situations no list covers.
depth.summary: Mat does two different jobs. As an expletive it reports the speaker's state, stands outside the clause and takes no arguments; as invective it makes a person the subject of an evaluation and lowers their standing in front of others. Syntax separates the two: a predicate of ты, an apposition, an imperative with a directional phrase or an agent noun targets a person, while a comma-separated word at the edge of a clause does not. Prefixes move the force along a scale from effect on a state through effect on interests and peace to public humiliation, and suffixes decide whether the evaluation lands on a mass, a person, a process or a situation. Diminutives and augmentatives change stance, not register. Classify by target and audience, not by a numerical score.

lessons.title: Audience is the variable: friends, strangers, the workplace, the family and the law
lessons.explanation:
The force of a mat expression is decided less by the word than by who is present. A sentence that draws laughter at a kitchen table can end a job at a reception desk, and the words do not change between the two rooms. What changes is the licence to use them, and licence is granted by relationship and setting rather than by dictionary. This lesson sets out the four settings an adult learner is most likely to meet, and the legal layer that sits underneath all of them.

Among friends, the licensing is reciprocal and historical. Zhelvis's taxonomy of invective functions, summarised in the Russian Wikipedia article on обсценная лексика (ap-STSEN-na-ya LEK-see-ka), 'obscene vocabulary', includes the function of establishing contact between equals and the function of friendly teasing or encouragement, alongside the function of lowering the addressee's status. Those first two are the ones at work among friends: the obscenity signals that the relationship is close enough to survive it, and the message is affiliation rather than aggression. The conditions are narrow. The speakers need a shared history, roughly equal standing, and a tone that everyone present reads the same way. A learner who observes the phenomenon and reproduces the words without the history is performing the signal without the relationship, which is why the same sentence that bonds two colleagues can sour a third.

Among strangers there is no licence at all, and the absence is not repaired by a smile. The same phrase that means 'we are close' to a friend means 'I am willing to attack you' to a stranger, because the status-lowering function is the only one available when no relationship exists. In a public place the consequence can be practical as well as social: an exchange that begins with an obscenity between strangers can escalate, and the person who started it is the one who will be described as having started it. Learners sometimes assume that a foreign accent buys tolerance. It buys confusion, and confusion does not reliably de-escalate.

The workplace adds an institution. What matters there is not the feelings of the people in the room but the register the institution is maintaining, which may be a client relationship, a professional standard or a public-facing brand. The exposure is institutional rather than statutory: an employer's internal rules, a client complaint and a written record do the work that a statute does elsewhere. Written channels raise the risk sharply because they persist. A spoken word in a corridor is remembered; a message is screenshotted, forwarded and read out at a meeting six months later. If a learner remembers one rule from this lesson, it should be that mat in a written channel belongs to the record and not to the conversation.

The family setting adds a third party who did not consent. The Russian legal frame here is the law on protecting children from information harmful to their health and development, which the Wikipedia article on мат summarises in its section on media restrictions. The summary distinguishes two tiers. Obscene language, which the article defines through Roskomnadzor's guidance as the four obscene names and all their derivatives, is barred outright. Swearing that is not classified as нецензурная брань (nee-tsen-ZOOR-na-ya BRAN'), 'obscene abuse', is permitted in print and online media with a 16+ marking, and on television and radio only after 21:00 local time. That two-tier structure is the clearest official statement of where Russian institutions draw the line, and it is the line lesson 138's ladder is built to cross.

The legal layer itself is administrative rather than criminal in the ordinary case. Article 20.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences, quoted in the same article, defines мелкое хулиганство (MYEL-ka-ye khoo-lee-GAN-stva), 'petty hooliganism', as a breach of public order expressing clear disrespect for society, accompanied by нецензурная брань in public places, by offensive harassment of citizens, or by the destruction or damage of other people's property, and it provides for a fine or administrative arrest. Part 3 of the same article extends the provision to information disseminated through telecommunications networks, including the internet, where it expresses clear disrespect for society, the state, official symbols, the constitution or the authorities in an indecent form. Parts 3 to 5 require the prosecutor's office to be notified within twenty-four hours. Enforcement is discretionary and uneven, which is exactly why a learner should not treat the statute as a threshold below which anything is permitted.

Four questions settle most cases before the words are chosen. Who is present, and have they consented to this register? Who can overhear, since a public place is defined by the possibility of an audience? Which institution governs the space, since a workplace, a school and a station have different rules and different record-keepers? And what will persist, since speech decays and text does not? If any answer is uncertain, the safe form is the one from the euphemism ladder in lesson 138, and the cost of using it is a slightly weaker joke.
lessons.example:
Take one sentence and move it through four rooms. The sentence is «Да пошёл ты» (da pa-SHYOL ty), 'well, get lost', which ids 21 to 30 already introduced as a rude dismissal. At a kitchen table between two old friends, after a disagreement about football, it is a move in a game: the tone is flat, both parties laugh, and nothing is at stake. On a street at night, addressed to a stranger who has bumped into you, the same words are an invitation to a fight, and the only variable that changed is the relationship. In an open-plan office, spoken across the desks to a colleague who has just contradicted you, the words are a status attack with an audience, and the audience is the problem even if the colleague laughs. In a written message to a client, the same words end the relationship and become evidence.

Now the same exercise with a stronger form. «Иди на хуй» (ee-DEE na KHUY), 'fuck off', among friends after a bad joke, is the kind of thing that gets repeated as an anecdote. Said to a stranger in a queue, it is the clearest possible invitation to escalation, and if the exchange becomes a disturbance, the phrase is the detail that identifies who began it. Written in a group chat that includes a manager, it is a disciplinary fact rather than a joke, because the manager did not consent to the register and now has a record. Written to a client, it is unrecoverable.

The analytic point is that the four rooms contain four different speech acts built from one sentence. In the first, the act is affiliation. In the second, it is aggression. In the third, it is a status attack in front of witnesses. In the fourth, it is a permanent institutional record. A learner who classifies the sentence as 'rude' has one label where four are needed, and the label does not tell them which room they are in. The practical habit is to name the room before naming the word.
lessons.question: A man tells a mat joke in a pub and his friends laugh. Twenty minutes later, outside, he uses the same words at a stranger who has bumped into him. What has changed, and why is the second use a different act?
lessons.answer: The licence has gone: among friends the obscenity signals affiliation, while at a stranger the only available function is lowering his status, which reads as aggression.
lessons.distractor: Nothing essential has changed, because the words are the same and the man's intention was humorous in both cases.
lessons.correction: The error is to locate meaning in the words rather than in the relationship. Zhelvis's list of invective functions includes both contact between equals and the lowering of an addressee's status; the first requires a shared history and roughly equal standing, and the second requires neither. With his friends, the man's obscenity selects the affiliation function because the relationship licenses it. At a stranger, that function is unavailable and the status-lowering one is what the hearer receives, whatever the speaker intended. Intention is not a defence in this analysis, because the hearer has no access to it. The practical consequence is that the same speaker can be harmless in one room and provocative in another without changing a single word, which is why lesson 137 classifies by audience rather than by vocabulary.

depth.definitions: Five terms do the work. Register is the variety of language a setting expects, and a mat expression is a register choice rather than a lexical one. Audience design is the process of shaping an utterance for the people who will hear it, including those who overhear it. A public place, in the administrative sense used by article 20.1, is a space where other people are present or can be, which is why a street and a station count and a private flat usually does not. нецензурная брань (nee-tsen-ZOOR-na-ya BRAN'), 'obscene abuse', is the legal category that the media rules treat as absolutely barred, as distinct from swearing that is merely rude. An administrative offence is a breach punishable by a fine or arrest rather than by a criminal penalty, and petty hooliganism is the one most often attached to public obscenity. Prerequisites are lesson 136 on target and force, and lesson 87 on disagreement without damage.
depth.mechanism:
Licensing works by reciprocity. Two speakers who have both used the register before, and who have both survived it, have established that the obscenity will be read as affiliation rather than attack. The licence is not a property of the word and it is not transferable: a third person who joins the conversation has not consented, and a change of setting removes the shared context even when the same people are present. That is why the pub and the street differ even for the same speaker on the same evening.

Institutions respond to records rather than to feelings. A workplace has rules, a client has a contract and a platform has terms of service, and all three operate on what can be shown. This is the mechanism behind the warning about written channels: a message converts a fleeting speech act into a document that can be re-read by people who were not there and who owe the speaker nothing. The same mechanism explains why the internet provision in article 20.1 part 3 exists at all.

The legal mechanism is categorical rather than gradual. The media rules do not weigh context; they name four obscene items and their derivatives and bar them, while permitting other swearing under age markings and time restrictions. That categorical structure is why the euphemism ladder matters: it is not a set of polite synonyms but a set of forms that sit on the permitted side of a legal line.
depth.secondExample: A reception desk, a queue and a telephone call, in one sequence. At the desk, a customer says «Вы что, издеваетесь?» (vy SHTA, eez-dee-VA-ye-tyes'), 'are you messing me about?', which is sharp and entirely publishable. The clerk, exhausted, mutters «Заебало всё это» (za-ye-BA-la VSYO EH-ta), 'I am sick of all this', to a colleague. The mutter has no target among the customers, and it is still a register failure in a public-facing role, because the customer can hear it. Now the same clerk on the telephone, to a supplier: «Вы уже третий раз срываете поставку» (vy oo-ZHE TRYE-tee ras sry-VA-ye-tye pa-STAFF-koo), 'this is the third time you have failed the delivery'. Firm, specific, no obscenity, and far more effective than the mutter, because it names the failure rather than the feeling. The lesson is not that the clerk should be politer; it is that the neutral form does more work in an institutional setting, where the record rather than the relationship carries the message.
depth.mistake:
The first error is to generalise from a tolerant audience. A learner hears mat at a dinner party, concludes that the register is available, and uses it at a work lunch with different people present. The licence was local and it does not travel. The diagnostic is to ask whether everyone present has heard you use the register before and reacted well; if the answer is no, the licence has not been granted.

The second error is to treat the law as the whole risk. Article 20.1 is the visible edge, and most of the damage happens well inside it: a client who stops replying, a manager who remembers, a relative who decides you are a certain kind of person. The third error is to import English norms. English swearing is tolerated in some professional and media registers where Russian mat is not, and a learner who translates register along with vocabulary will misjudge both the workplace and the family table.
depth.application:
Before speaking, run the four questions: who is present, who can overhear, which institution governs the space, what will persist. In a written channel, add a fifth: would you be content for this to be read aloud by someone you have not met? If the answer is no, the form is unavailable, and the euphemism ladder supplies a replacement that keeps the emotional content while removing the legal and institutional exposure.

If you misjudge and the room goes cold, the repair is short and specific. «Извините, я неудачно пошутил» (eez-vee-NEE-tye, ya nee-DACH-na pa-shoo-TEEL), 'sorry, that joke landed badly', acknowledges the misjudgement without arguing about the words, and it works because it names the act rather than the vocabulary. What does not work is explaining that the word is common among your friends, which tells the room that you have misread it rather than that you regret it.
depth.summary: Force depends on audience. Among friends, mat can signal affiliation and teasing, because a shared history licenses it; among strangers the same words can only lower status, which reads as aggression. Workplaces add institutional rules, client relationships and permanent records, and written channels convert speech into evidence. The family setting adds people who did not consent, and Russian law handles it through the two-tier media rule, which bars the four obscene items outright and permits other swearing under age markings and time limits. Article 20.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences makes public obscenity a form of petty hooliganism punishable by fine or arrest, and part 3 extends it to the internet. Classify the room before you classify the word.

lessons.title: The euphemism ladder: блин, ёлки-палки, пипец, фиг, хрен and what each one replaces
lessons.explanation:
A minced oath is a harmless expression substituted for a taboo one, usually because it sounds similar. The English Wikipedia article on the subject treats the device as a general feature of languages under taboo, and Russian has an unusually well-developed set of them for mat, because the legal and social cost of the obscene form is high enough to make deniability valuable. The ladder in this lesson is the practical result: a series of rungs from the obscene word to a form that can be printed, each one mapped onto the word it replaces.

The блядь chain was described in lesson 135 and is the model. блядь (BLYAT') is the obscene form; бля (BLYA) is the clipped exclamation, still obscene; бляха (BLYA-kha) is a real noun meaning a buckle plate or badge, recorded by the English Wiktionary entry as a minced oath especially in бляха-муха (BLYA-kha MOO-kha); блин (BLEEN) is the word for a pancake and the mildest rung. Each step keeps the opening consonant cluster and the single syllable, so the hearer reconstructs the taboo word while hearing something publishable. That is the mechanism in one sentence: recognition is preserved, deniability is gained.

The пиздец chain is shorter and blunter. пипец (pee-PYETS) is recorded in the English Wiktionary entry as a euphemistic and vulgar substitute for пиздец (peez-DYETS), used both for an extreme degree of something and as an exclamation of disaster, with писец (pee-SYETS), песец (pee-SYETS) and капец (ka-PYETS) listed as further variants. The entry's label matters: euphemistic and vulgar at the same time. A euphemism lowers the legal exposure; it does not make the word polite, and пипец in a formal document still reads as swearing.

The хуй chain runs through two substitutes. фиг (FEEK) is the name of a hand gesture, a fist with the thumb thrust between the index and middle fingers, which the English Wiktionary entry identifies as the fig sign and equates with кукиш (KOO-keesh) and шиш (SHEESH); it is a vulgar gesture in its own right, which is why the word works as a substitute. The same entry records the fixed expressions ни фига (nee fee-GA) and до фига (da fee-GA), and it adds a stress note that is worth memorising: in both expressions the final syllable is stressed, unlike the bare word. From the same root come фигня (feeg-NYA), 'nonsense, junk', and пофиг (PO-feek), 'it is all the same to me'. хрен (KHRYEN) is the other substitute, literally horseradish, and it generates хреново (khrye-NO-va), 'badly', хрен знает (khryen ZNA-yet), 'nobody knows, the hell knows', and на хрен (na KHRYEN), 'to hell with it'. Both фиг and хрен are the standard replacements for хуй in dismissals, which is why иди на фиг (ee-DEE na FEEK) exists as the publishable version of a phrase already taught at id 26.

The interjection chain replaces the whole formula rather than a single root. ёлки-палки (YOL-kee PAL-kee) is recorded by English Wiktionary as a minced oath of mild dismay, glossed 'fiddlesticks', with ёлки-моталки (YOL-kee ma-TAL-kee) and ё-моё (yo ma-YO) as synonyms. It stands in for ёб твою мать (YOB tva-YU MAT') without sharing a single morpheme, which shows that the device does not always need phonetic resemblance: what it needs is a comparable shape and a comparable emotional slot.

The ladder is also a censorship boundary, and this is the part that makes it more than a style guide. Roskomnadzor's guidance, summarised in the Wikipedia article on мат, bars the four obscene names and all their derivatives from Russian media, and it adds that replacing letters with ellipsis does not remove liability, though a formulation such as 'the word beginning with b' is acceptable. Swearing that is not classified as нецензурная брань (nee-tsen-ZOOR-na-ya BRAN'), 'obscene abuse', is permitted in print and online media with a 16+ marking and on broadcast after 21:00. Every rung of the ladder above бля sits on the permitted side of that line. That is the mapping the lesson asks for: блядь is barred, бля is barred, бляха and блин are permitted with markings, пиздец is barred, пипец is permitted but vulgar, хуй is barred, фиг and хрен are permitted.

The trap is to hear the ladder as a politeness scale. It is a deniability scale. The pragmatic force is largely preserved, which is why блин can carry real irritation and why пипец can be a genuine complaint; the taboo is reduced, not the feeling. Digit substitution works the same way, and the English Wiktionary entry for пизда records 3.14зда as a texting spelling, which shows that speakers treat the substitution as transparent. A reader reconstructs the original instantly, and so does a regulator.
lessons.example:
One situation at six rungs: a train has been cancelled and you are late. Rung one, the obscene form: «Пиздец, поезд отменили.» (peez-DYETS, PO-yezd at-mee-NEE-lee) 'Disaster, the train is cancelled.' Barred from any published text and risky in a public place. Rung two: «Пипец, поезд отменили.» (pee-PYETS, PO-yezd at-mee-NEE-lee) The same sentence with a euphemism; it can be printed with an age marking, and it still sounds like swearing. Rung three: «Блин, поезд отменили.» (BLEEN, PO-yezd at-mee-NEE-lee) 'Darn, the train is cancelled.' Perfectly ordinary in almost any company.

Now the dismissal, which has its own ladder. «Иди на хуй» (ee-DEE na KHUY) is the obscene form. «Иди на фиг» (ee-DEE na FEEK) is publishable and still rude. «Да ну тебя» (da noo tee-BYA) is not a euphemism at all but a neutral refusal to continue, and it shows the limit of the device: at some point you stop substituting and start saying something else. The interjection ladder runs «Ёб твою мать» (YOB tva-YU MAT'), then «Ёлки-палки» (YOL-kee PAL-kee), then «Ну надо же» (noo NA-da zhe), 'well, would you believe it'.

Three observations close the example. The first is that the rungs are not interchangeable in tone: блин is mild and slightly resigned, пипец is harsh and often comic, фиг is dismissive, хрен is rural and blunt. The second is that the ladder changes the legal position, not the emotional one; the frustration is the same at every rung. The third is that the neutral paraphrase, «поезд отменили, я опаздываю» (PO-yezd at-mee-NEE-lee, ya a-paz-DY-va-yu), 'the train is cancelled and I am late', is the only form that carries information without any register at all, and in a written message to someone who owes you nothing it is the best of the six.
lessons.question: You need to tell a colleague in a work chat that a delivery has failed badly. Which form belongs there, and which substitution only looks safe?
lessons.answer: Пипец or a plain statement such as «поставка сорвалась» (pa-STAFF-ka sar-VA-las'), 'the delivery fell through'; the obscene word and its asterisked or digit-substituted versions do not belong.
lessons.distractor: Пиздец with asterisks, because masking the letters removes the obscenity while keeping the emphasis.
lessons.correction: Masking does not change the word for the reader, and it does not change it for a regulator either: Roskomnadzor's guidance, as summarised in the Wikipedia article on мат, states that replacing letters with ellipsis does not remove liability, while a formulation such as 'the word beginning with b' is acceptable precisely because it does not reproduce the word. Asterisks also fail the social test, since the reader reconstructs the original instantly and the emphasis is preserved while the deniability is not. пипец is the genuine substitute and it is permitted with markings, though it is labelled both euphemistic and vulgar, so in a formal message the plain statement is better still. The learner's error is to think that censorship is a matter of typography rather than of which word is present.

depth.definitions: Five terms. A euphemism is a mild expression substituted for a harsher one. A minced oath is a euphemism for a taboo word or formula, usually similar in sound, and бляха and блин are the Russian examples. Censorship is the removal or prohibition of material by an authority, and the Russian media rules are an instance. Deniability is the property of a form that cannot be quoted against the speaker as the obscenity itself. Register is the variety a setting expects, and the ladder is a set of register choices rather than a set of synonyms. Prerequisites are lesson 135 on the блядь chain, lesson 132 on the хуй family, and lesson 137 on the legal layer.
depth.mechanism:
Two mechanisms make the ladder work. The first is phonetic resemblance: the substitute keeps enough of the taboo word's sound for the hearer to reconstruct it, which preserves the emphasis. The second is lexical independence: the substitute is a real word with its own meaning, so it can appear in print without being the obscenity. бляха is a buckle, блин is a pancake, фиг is a gesture, хрен is horseradish, and each is a normal noun in its own right.

Where resemblance is impossible, the ladder uses functional equivalence instead. ёлки-палки shares nothing with ёб твою мать except its shape as an exclamation and its emotional slot, and it works because exclamations are identified by function rather than by content. That is why the interjection ladder can be shorter than the noun ladders without breaking.

The legal mechanism is categorical. The rules name four obscene items and their derivatives and bar them, which means that the ladder's rungs either contain one of those roots or do not. бля contains бля, so it is barred. бляха does not, so it is permitted with a marking. That binary structure is why the ladder is a reliable guide to publication and an unreliable guide to politeness.
depth.secondExample:
Two channels, one frustration. In a bar, after a match is lost: «Пиздец, ну и игра.» (peez-DYETS, noo ee ee-GRA) 'Disaster, what a game.' Among friends, the obscene form is the ordinary one. In a work chat, the same frustration: «Пипец, поставку опять перенесли.» (pee-PYETS, pa-STAFF-koo a-PYAT' pee-ree-nee-SLEE) 'Bloody hell, the delivery has been postponed again.' The euphemism is permitted and the register is still recognisably exasperated. In a formal report, the same event: «Поставка перенесена на неделю, это ставит под угрозу срок сдачи.» (pa-STAFF-ka pee-ree-nee-SYE-na na nee-DYE-lyu, EH-ta STA-veet pat oog-RO-zoo SROK SDA-chee) 'The delivery has been postponed by a week, which puts the deadline at risk.' No obscenity, no euphemism, and more authority than either.

The progression is not from rude to polite but from personal to institutional. Each step removes a little of the speaker's state and adds a little of the situation's facts. A learner who can move along that progression deliberately has a wider range than one who has memorised a single substitute.
depth.mistake:
The first error is to treat euphemism as politeness. пипец is a euphemism and it is still vulgar; блин is mild and can still be a verbal tic that irritates the people around you. The register moves down the ladder, not to the bottom of it. The second error is to think that masking is substitution. Asterisks, digits and initial letters either reproduce the word, in which case they do not protect the writer, or they do not, in which case the reader has to guess and the emphasis is lost. The only masking form the guidance explicitly permits is naming the letter without the word.

The third error is over-generalising a rung. Learners who discover блин use it in every register, including formal writing, where it reads as a lapse of control rather than as emphasis. The fourth is assuming that the ladder covers every obscenity. It covers the four barred roots and the interjection formula; it does not supply substitutes for insults aimed at people, because there is no deniable way to insult someone, which is the point lesson 139 takes up.
depth.application:
Choose a rung by answering two questions: who will read or hear this, and what happens if they quote it back? In speech among peers, the lower rungs are available. In writing that will be filed, only the neutral paraphrase is really safe. In public speech, the legal line runs between бля and бляха, and between пиздец and пипец, and a speaker who knows where the line is can be emphatic without being exposed.

For comprehension, the ladder is a decoding tool. When you hear пипец, блин, фиг or хрен, reconstruct the word underneath and you will know the emotional temperature of the sentence, which is usually more useful than a literal gloss. The substitutes are frequent in film dialogue and in interviews precisely because they are publishable, and a learner who does not recognise them will miss most of the frustration in a Russian comedy.
depth.summary: The euphemism ladder replaces taboo forms with real words of similar shape, preserving recognition while gaining deniability. блядь runs through бля and бляха to блин; пиздец is replaced by пипец, писец, песец and капец; хуй is replaced by фиг and хрен, with ни фига and до фига stressed on the final syllable; the interjection formula is replaced by ёлки-палки. The ladder is also the media boundary: the four obscene items and their derivatives are barred, while the substitutes are permitted with age markings and time limits, and ellipsis or asterisk masking does not remove liability. Euphemism lowers exposure, not feeling, and the neutral paraphrase remains the only form with no register at all.

lessons.title: When someone swears at you: не надо так, давай спокойно, я не понял, ты чего, and the limit that is not submission
lessons.explanation:
An insult aimed at you is a move in an exchange, and the reply determines whether the exchange continues. Four short phrases cover most of the ground an adult learner needs, and they are graded by firmness rather than by politeness. The first is не надо так (nee NA-da tak), 'don't do that'. It is impersonal, it uses не надо plus the adverb так, and it names the behaviour instead of the person. The second is давай спокойно (da-VAY spa-KOY-na), 'let's stay calm', where давай plus an adverb forms a first person plural imperative, the same construction as давай пойдём (da-VAY pa-YDYOM), 'let's go'; the formal or plural version is давайте спокойно (da-VAY-tye spa-KOY-na). The third is я не понял (ya ne PO-nyal), 'I did not catch that', with я не поняла (ya ne pa-NYA-la) for a female speaker. The fourth is ты чего? (ty chee-VO), 'what is with you?', which is colloquial and only possible with ты.

The four are not interchangeable, and the difference is register rather than meaning. не надо так is soft and slightly supervisory; said to a peer it can sound as if you are correcting a child, which is why it works best from a position of some authority or in a calm, low voice. давай спокойно is conciliatory and managerial at once: it proposes a joint course of action and implies that the other person is currently not calm, which is a small accusation in itself. я не понял is the firmest of the four because it is a repair move. It asks the speaker to repeat what they said, which forces them to hear it again and to decide whether to own it, and it gives them a face-saving exit if they choose to withdraw. ты чего is familiar and can defuse a misunderstanding between peers, but used at a stranger it sounds like a challenge, because ты itself is an intimacy claim.

The pronoun is part of the message. Russian's second person singular and plural carry the distinction that the English Wikipedia article on the T–V distinction describes in terms of power and solidarity: вы marks distance, formality or respect, and ты marks closeness, either affectionate or contemptuous. When a stranger swears at you with ты, the pronoun is already an insult, because it claims an intimacy that has not been granted. Your reply can either accept that frame or refuse it. Moving to вы, as in я вас не понял (ya vas ne PO-nyal), 'I did not catch you', creates distance without aggression, and it is often more effective than any content word. Keeping ты signals that you accept the exchange as one between equals, which is appropriate with a colleague and risky with a stranger.

The central distinction of the lesson is between de-escalation and submission. De-escalation lowers the temperature of the exchange while keeping the limit in place. Submission accepts the treatment and drops the limit. The two look similar in the first ten seconds because both involve a calm voice and no counter-insult, and they diverge afterwards: de-escalation ends with the behaviour stopped or the exchange ended, while submission ends with the behaviour continuing. The practical test is whether you state the limit once, plainly, and then act on it. «Я не буду это слушать» (ya ne BOO-doo EH-ta SLOO-shat'), 'I am not going to listen to this', is a limit. «Ну ладно, ладно» (noo LAD-na, LAD-na), 'all right, all right', is a submission, because it accepts the continuation.

What not to do is as important as what to do. Mirroring the obscenity raises the temperature and hands the other person a justification; laughing it off tells everyone present that the behaviour is acceptable; lecturing about language is a status move that invites a counter-move; and apologising for something you did not do teaches the other person that pressure works. The one exception is a genuine misjudgement on your part, which deserves a short, specific apology and then a return to the point.

The phrases also have a diagnostic use. If the swearing is not aimed at you, as when someone spills coffee and swears at the world, no reply is required and any reply is an escalation. Lesson 136's test applies: is there a second person subject or an imperative addressed to you? If not, the expletive is about the speaker's state, and the appropriate response is none. If there is, the four phrases above are the repertoire, and the choice among them is a choice of how much distance you want to create.
lessons.example:
Three scenes, three replies. Scene one, a bus stop, a drunk man who has been muttering turns to you: «Ты чего вылупился, хуй?» (ty chee-VO VY-loo-peel-sya, KHUY) 'What are you staring at, prick?' The obscenity is aimed at you, the ты claims intimacy, and the question invites a defence. The reply that lowers the temperature without accepting the frame is «Я вас не понял» (ya vas ne PO-nyal), 'I did not catch you', with the вы doing most of the work, followed by physical distance: step back, turn slightly away, keep your voice level. If he repeats it, «Я не буду это слушать» (ya ne BOO-doo EH-ta SLOO-shat') and leave. What not to say is «Иди на хуй» (ee-DEE na KHUY), which matches his register, gives him a reason to escalate and, in a public place, converts a nuisance into a disturbance in which you are a participant.

Scene two, an office, a colleague who has just lost an argument says «Да ты вообще хуйню говоришь» (da ty va-ap-SHCHY khooy-NYOO ga-vo-REESH), 'what you are saying is complete crap'. The words are aimed at your contribution rather than at your person, which is a lower grade of attack, and the audience is the team. «Давай спокойно» (da-VAY spa-KOY-na) works here because the relationship is peer and continuing, and it invites the colleague to rejoin the discussion rather than to defend a character. Add the substantive move: «Давай спокойно. Вот данные, посмотри.» (da-VAY spa-KOY-na. vot DAN-ny-ye, pa-sma-TREE) 'Let us stay calm. Here are the figures, look.'

Scene three, a family table, an older relative uses a mat expression about your plans. The target is your plan, not you, and the audience is the family. не надо так is the right grade, and it should be said quietly and once. If it continues, the limit moves from the words to the setting: «Я не буду это обсуждать за столом» (ya ne BOO-doo EH-ta ap-sooZH-DAT' za sta-LOM), 'I am not going to discuss this at the table.' That is a boundary about behaviour, and it can be acted on by changing the subject or leaving the room.
lessons.question: At a bus stop a stranger swears at you and uses ты. Which reply keeps the limit without escalating, and why is matching his words the wrong move?
lessons.answer: «Я вас не понял» (ya vas ne PO-nyal), 'I did not catch you', with the вы creating distance, followed by stepping away; matching his obscenity escalates and makes you a participant in the disturbance.
lessons.distractor: «Иди на хуй» (ee-DEE na KHUY), because answering in the same register shows that you are not intimidated.
lessons.correction: Matching the register is the single most common error, and it fails on two counts. Socially, it converts a one-sided aggression into a mutual exchange, which is what the aggressor wanted and what bystanders will later describe. Legally, in a public place it turns a nuisance into a disturbance, and article 20.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences treats public obscenity as petty hooliganism, so the person who answers in kind becomes part of the offence rather than its victim. The вы in я вас не понял does the work that a counter-insult cannot: it refuses the intimacy that his ты claimed, it asks him to repeat himself in front of witnesses, and it leaves him the option of withdrawing. De-escalation here is not surrender, because the limit is still stated and the exit is still taken.

depth.definitions: Five terms. Invective is language that attacks a target and lowers their standing. De-escalation is the reduction of the intensity of a conflict without conceding the substance. A boundary is a statement of what you will do, as distinct from a demand that the other person change. Face is the public self-image that an exchange can threaten, and the T–V distinction is the choice between singular and plural second person that marks distance or closeness. Prerequisites are lesson 136 on target and force, lesson 137 on audience, and lesson 97 on requests and address forms.
depth.mechanism:
я не понял works because it is a repair move rather than a counter-attack. Conversation analysis treats repair as the machinery by which participants fix trouble in talk, and asking for repetition makes the other person the author of the trouble: they must either repeat the insult, which is now deliberate, or withdraw it. It also buys time, which lowers the temperature, and it gives the aggressor a socially acceptable exit, which is often what they need in front of witnesses.

Matching the obscenity works in the opposite direction because aggression is reciprocal. An insult answered by an insult establishes that both parties are willing to escalate, and the exchange then has no natural stopping point. The audience matters here: an exchange with witnesses rewards the person who appears calm and punishes the person who appears to have lost control, which is why the calm reply is also the stronger social move.

A boundary works because it is behavioural. A demand such as 'stop swearing' asks the other person to change and gives them the power to refuse; a statement such as 'I am not going to listen to this' describes what you will do and can be carried out without their consent. That is the mechanism behind the claim that de-escalation is not submission: the temperature falls, and the limit is still enforced by your own action.
depth.secondExample:
A workplace version, with a manager present. A colleague says, in a meeting, «Это полная хуйня, и ты это знаешь» (EH-ta POL-na-ya khooy-NYA, ee ty EH-ta ZNA-yesh), 'this is complete crap and you know it'. The audience makes the status attack serious, and the manager's presence makes the reply a public act. «Я не понял. Ты о чём?» (ya ne PO-nyal. ty a CHYOM) 'I did not catch that. What are you referring to?' The repair move forces the colleague to specify, and the specification is usually less aggressive than the original, because specifics can be answered. If the colleague repeats the obscenity, the limit is procedural rather than emotional: «Давай вернёмся к цифрам» (da-VAY veer-NYOM-sya k TSEEF-ram), 'let us go back to the figures', which returns the exchange to the institutional frame where the manager's presence is an advantage rather than a liability.

Note what the reply does not do. It does not deny the substance, so it cannot be read as weakness; it does not match the register, so it cannot be read as escalation; and it does not ask the colleague to apologise, so it leaves them a way back into the meeting. Those three properties are what make it a de-escalation rather than a submission, and they can be transferred to almost any setting where an audience is present.
depth.mistake:
The first error is the mirror. Learners who have just acquired mat vocabulary are tempted to use it under pressure, and the temptation is strongest exactly when the register is hostile. The result is a mutual exchange in which the learner's Russian is at its least controlled and the audience's sympathy is at its least reliable.

The second error is over-apologising. «Извините, извините, я не хотел» (eez-vee-NEE-tye, eez-vee-NEE-tye, ya ne kha-TYEL), 'sorry, sorry, I did not mean it', accepts blame for an act you did not commit and invites more pressure. The third error is to treat calm as agreement. A low voice and a stated limit are not the same as a concession, and a learner who confuses the two will either escalate to prove they are not weak or submit to keep the peace. The distinction is behavioural: what you do after the sentence decides which one it was.
depth.application:
Keep the four phrases available as a small repertoire and choose by audience. With a stranger, вы plus я не понял plus distance. With a peer, давай спокойно plus the substantive point. With family, не надо так said once quietly, then a behavioural limit. With a friend who is teasing, ты чего, because the intimacy is real and the register is shared.

In every case, decide the exit before you speak: step away, end the call, leave the room, or involve a third party. An exit that you have already chosen is what makes the calm sentence a boundary rather than a plea. If the situation involves threats or physical risk, the exit comes first and the sentence is optional, because no phrase is worth a confrontation with someone who is looking for one.
depth.summary: Four phrases cover the reply to an insult: не надо так, давай спокойно, я не понял and ты чего, graded from supervisory through conciliatory and firm to familiar. The pronoun carries as much as the phrase, since ты claims intimacy and вы creates distance, and a stranger's ты is itself part of the attack. The firmest reply is the repair move, because it makes the other person repeat or withdraw. De-escalation is not submission: it lowers the temperature and keeps the limit, and the limit is behavioural, stated once and then acted on. Matching the obscenity escalates socially and, in a public place, can make you part of the offence.

lessons.title: Capstone: reading an exchange for target, force and register, and producing the safe reply
lessons.explanation:
This lesson puts the unit together on one invented exchange. The method has three labels and an order. First decide the target: is a person being evaluated, or is the speaker reporting their own state, or is a thing being evaluated? Second decide the force: is the act an expletive, an evaluation, an intrusion, a humiliation, a dismissal or an order? Third decide the register: who is present, who can overhear, and what institution governs the space? The order matters, because a word's dictionary label tells you almost nothing until the first two questions are answered, and the third question can change the answer to the first.

The exchange is between two colleagues in a work chat. Colleague A writes «Ты опять не прислал смету» (ty a-PYAT' ne pree-SLAL SMYE-too), 'you have not sent the estimate again'. Colleague B replies «Да блядь, я её вчера отправил» (da BLYAT', ya ye-YO fchee-RA at-PRA-veel'), 'for fuck's sake, I sent it yesterday'. A answers «Не надо так со мной разговаривать» (nee NA-da tak sa MNOY raz-GA-va-ree-vat'), 'do not talk to me like that'. B says «Да ладно, это же просто слово» (da LAD-na, EH-ta zhe PRO-sta SLO-va), 'come on, it is just a word'. A replies «Я не понял. Ты это мне?» (ya ne PO-nyal. ty EH-ta mnye), 'I did not catch that. Is that aimed at me?' B closes with «Нет, не тебе. Извини, день тяжёлый» (nyet, ne tee-BYE. eez-vee-NEE, dyen' tee-ZHO-ly), 'no, not at you. Sorry, rough day.'

Classify it turn by turn. Turn one is a factual reproach with no obscenity, and its force is a complaint about a task. Turn two contains the strongest single word in the exchange and its target is nobody: блядь (BLYAT') stands at the head of the clause, set off by a comma, and the clause is a complete statement without it. The force is an expletive, and the register is the problem, because the channel is a workplace system even though the relationship is peer to peer. Turn three is not an insult and not an escalation; it is a boundary, and its force is procedural. Turn four is a denial of harm, which is the commonest move available to someone who has just misjudged a register: it reframes the objection as oversensitivity. Turn five is the repair move from lesson 139, and it does the analytic work the whole lesson is about, because it forces the classification question out loud. Turn six is a withdrawal with an account, and it resolves the exchange without either party losing standing.

The counterfactual makes the method visible. Suppose turn two had been «Ты блядь» (ty BLYAT'), with the same word in the predicate slot of the second person pronoun. Everything else in the exchange could stay identical and the classification would change completely: the target becomes the hearer, the force becomes an insult to standing, and the register question changes its answer, because an insult in a workplace channel is an institutional fact rather than a lapse of tone. The same letters, two different speech acts, and the difference is entirely syntactic. That is why lesson 136 insisted on the removal test and why this capstone asks for labels rather than for a severity score.

The second exchange moves the same method to a public place. A stranger at a bus stop says «Ты чего вылупился, хуй?» (ty chee-VO VY-loo-peel-sya, KHUY), 'what are you staring at, prick?' The target is you, the pronoun claims an intimacy that has not been granted, and the force is a challenge with an insult attached. The safe reply is «Я вас не понял» (ya vas ne PO-nyal), 'I did not catch you', with the вы creating distance, followed by physical movement away. If the stranger continues, «Я не буду это слушать» (ya ne BOO-doo EH-ta SLOO-shat') and the exit. Nothing in that reply matches the register, and nothing in it concedes the limit.

Finally, the production side. The neutral rewrite of the first exchange is a writing exercise, not a moral one: it asks you to say the same things without the obscenity and without losing the information. That is the skill an adult learner actually needs, because the situations that require it are the ones with consequences. A rewrite that removes the frustration as well as the word is a failure; a rewrite that keeps the frustration and removes the word is the target.
lessons.example:
Read the exchange aloud twice, once for meaning and once for labels, then write the labels in the margin. Turn one: reproach, no obscenity, target is a task, register neutral. Turn two: expletive, no target, register obscene in an institutional channel. Turn three: boundary, target is the behaviour, register professional. Turn four: denial of harm, target is the objection, register defensive. Turn five: repair, target is the utterance, register firm and formal enough to be quotable. Turn six: withdrawal, target is the speaker's own behaviour, register conciliatory. Six turns, six labels, and only one of them contains mat.

Now test the counterfactual. Rewrite turn two as «Ты блядь» (ty BLYAT'), 'you are a whore' and re-label. Target: the hearer. Force: insult to standing. Register: obscene plus institutional plus a written record. The reply that follows would no longer be «Не надо так» (nee NA-da tak), 'don't do that', which is calibrated for tone, but a boundary about conduct, and the exchange would move from a misunderstanding to a personnel matter. Then rewrite turn two as «Бляха, я её вчера отправил» (BLYA-kha, ya ye-YO fchee-RA at-PRA-veel') and re-label again: the target is still nobody, the force is still an expletive, and the register drops below the line that the media rules draw, which is why the same sentence could appear in a published interview. Three versions of one turn, three different classifications, and the differences are one word and one comma.

The second exchange gets the same treatment. Turn one, the stranger: target is you, force is a challenge, register is public and non-consensual. Your reply: target is the utterance, force is a repair, register is formal because вы. His possible repeat: escalation. Your exit: behavioural, not verbal. Write the four steps in the margin and the scene becomes a procedure rather than a confrontation, which is the point of doing this on paper before doing it in a bus queue.
lessons.question: In the work-chat exchange, which turn contains invective, and what would change if a manager were added to the chat before turn two?
lessons.answer: Turn two contains an expletive, not invective, because its target is nobody; adding a manager does not change the target or the force, but it changes the register, because the obscenity becomes an institutional record rather than a lapse between peers.
lessons.distractor: Turn two contains invective because the word is obscene, and adding a manager changes nothing, since the participants are the same.
lessons.correction: The error is to read the word rather than the frame. блядь at the head of the clause, comma-separated, with a complete clause after it, is an expletive: remove it and the sentence still works, so it was never doing grammatical work against the hearer. That is why the label is expletive and the target is nobody. The manager's arrival does not alter either label, and it does alter the register, because the audience now includes someone with institutional authority and the channel now has a reader who did not consent to the tone. The distinction matters practically: a learner who labels turn two as invective will respond as if attacked, escalate a misunderstanding, and miss the actual problem, which is that a written workplace channel is the wrong place for the register.

depth.definitions: Four labels carry the capstone. Target is the person an utterance is aimed at, which may be nobody. Force is the kind of act performed, whether expletive, evaluation, intrusion, humiliation, dismissal or order. Register is the variety the setting requires, determined by who is present, who can overhear and which institution governs the space. Repair is the conversational move that fixes trouble in talk, and я не понял is the Russian example used here. A counterfactual is a deliberate change to one element of an exchange in order to see which labels move, and it is the fastest way to check that a classification is doing real work. Prerequisites are lessons 136 to 139.
depth.mechanism:
The method works because each label answers a different question and the questions are ordered. Target is decided by syntax: a second person subject, an imperative addressed to the hearer, an apposition or an agent noun makes a person the target, and nothing else does. Force is decided by the frame: an element outside the clause reports a state, a predicate evaluates, a transitive verb with a person in the accusative describes an effect, and an imperative with a direction orders movement. Register is decided by the setting: who is present, who can overhear, what rules apply and what persists.

The counterfactual is the check. Change one element and see which labels move. Replacing блядь with бляха leaves target and force unchanged and moves only the register, which tells you that the substitution is a register operation. Replacing «Да блядь» (da BLYAT'), 'for fuck's sake' with «Ты блядь» (ty BLYAT'), 'you are a whore' changes the target and the force and leaves the register where it was, which tells you that the syntactic change is the significant one. If a change moves no labels, the analysis has not found the operative feature yet.

The production step follows the same logic in reverse. Decide the register you need, then choose a form that sits inside it without losing the information, and check that the target and force you intended are the ones the form will deliver. That is why the neutral rewrite keeps the frustration: the force is part of the message, and removing it produces a text that is polite and useless.
depth.secondExample:
Here is the neutral rewrite of the work-chat exchange, keeping the information and dropping the register. A writes «Смету я пока не получил. Ты её отправил?» (SMYE-too ya pa-KA ne pa-loo-CHEEL. ty ye-YO at-PRA-veel) 'I have not received the estimate yet. Did you send it?' B replies «Отправил вчера, проверь, пожалуйста, почту, возможно, попало в спам» (at-PRA-veel fchee-RA, pra-VYER', pa-ZHA-loo-sta, POCH-too, vaz-MOZH-na, pa-PA-la f spam) 'I sent it yesterday, please check your mail, it may have gone to spam.' A answers «Проверю. Если не найду, пришли ещё раз» (pra-VYE-ryu. YEHS-lee ne NAY-doo, pree-SHLEE ye-SHCHYO ras) 'I will check. If I cannot find it, send it again.' B closes «Хорошо, отправлю копию» (kha-ra-SHO, at-PRAV-lyu KO-pee-yu) 'Fine, I will send a copy.'

Compare the two versions turn by turn. The reproach in turn one becomes a statement of fact plus a question, which removes the accusation without removing the request. The expletive in turn two disappears and the frustration is carried by the urgency of the request to check the mail. The boundary in turn three becomes unnecessary, because there is nothing to bound. The denial of harm in turn four disappears. The repair move in turn five becomes a plan. Nothing was added, nothing was moralised, and every fact in the original survives. That is what a register rewrite looks like when it is done for information rather than for propriety.
depth.mistake:
The first error is to classify by vocabulary. Learners label every sentence containing mat as invective, which makes them respond to expletives as attacks and miss real attacks that contain no mat at all, such as a calm and deliberate humiliation in neutral words. The second error is to forget the register question. A correct target and force with the wrong register is still a failure, as turn two of the exchange shows: nobody was attacked and the message was still a problem, because it was written in a channel that records.

The third error is to accept the denial of harm. «Это же просто слово» (EH-ta zhe PRO-sta SLO-va), 'it is just a word', is a move that relocates the problem from the speaker's conduct to the hearer's sensitivity, and a learner who agrees in order to keep the peace has conceded the register question. The fourth error is the opposite: treating a genuine expletive as a conduct issue, which turns a bad day into a grievance and teaches everyone present that the learner cannot read a room.
depth.application:
Use the three labels on any exchange you meet, and use the counterfactual when the labels feel uncertain. In reading, this turns a wall of subtitled dialogue into a sequence of speech acts with targets. In listening, it tells you which obscenities to ignore, because they are about the speaker, and which to answer, because they are about you. In production, it gives you a filter that works in situations no word list covers.

The transferable habit is the order: target, force, register, response. It takes about ten seconds, it needs no vocabulary beyond what lessons 131 to 139 supplied, and it scales from a bus stop to a board meeting. The written exercise is the same habit in slow motion, and it is worth doing once on paper for an exchange that actually happened to you, because the rewrite shows which information you were carrying with the obscenity and which you were using it to avoid saying.
depth.summary: The capstone method is three labels in a fixed order: target, then force, then register. Target is decided by syntax, force by the frame, register by audience and institution. The work-chat exchange shows an expletive with no target, a boundary that is not an insult, a denial of harm that must not be accepted, and a repair move that resolves the exchange. The counterfactual shows that the same word in a predicate slot becomes invective, and that a euphemism moves only the register. The bus-stop exchange shows the same method in public, with вы creating distance and the exit carrying the limit. The neutral rewrite keeps the information and the frustration and removes the register, which is the production skill the whole unit has been building.
